paragraphs: But Kolya did not hear her. At last he was free to go. Out at the gate he glanced around, hunched his shoulders, and said, “It’s freezing.” Then he walked straight down the street and turned right toward the market square. He stopped at the gate of the last house but one before the square, took a whistle from his pocket, and blew it with all his strength, as if giving a signal. He waited barely a minute. Then a rosy-cheeked boy of about eleven came darting out to meet him, in a warm, neat, even stylish coat. This was Smurov, a boy in the preparatory class (two classes below Kolya Krassotkin) and the son of a well-to-do official. His parents seemed to have forbidden him to keep company with Krassotkin, who was known to be a hopelessly naughty boy. So Smurov had plainly slipped out on the sly. He was—if the reader has not forgotten—one of the group of boys who had thrown stones at Ilusha two months before. He was the one who had told Alyosha Karamazov about Ilusha.
“I’ve been waiting for you for a whole hour, Krassotkin,” said Smurov flatly, and the two boys set off toward the market square.
“I’m late,” answered Krassotkin. “Circumstances held me up. You won’t be thrashed for coming with me, will you?”
“Oh, come on, I’m never thrashed! Have you brought Perezvon?”
“Yes.”
“You’re taking him along too?”
“Yes.”
“Ah, if only it were Zhutchka!”
“Impossible. Zhutchka doesn’t exist. Zhutchka has vanished into the mists of obscurity.”

“Ah, couldn’t we try something?” Smurov suddenly stopped. “Ilusha says Zhutchka was a shaggy, grayish, smoky-looking dog, just like Perezvon. Couldn’t you tell him this is Zhutchka? He might believe you.”
“Boy, steer clear of lies. That’s one thing. And even a lie told for a good purpose is another matter. Above all, I hope you haven’t told them I’m coming.”

“Heaven forbid! I know what I’m about. But Perezvon won’t comfort him,” said Smurov with a sigh. “You know his father, the captain, ‘the wisp of tow,’ told us he’d bring Ilusha a real mastiff pup today, with a black nose. He thinks that will cheer Ilusha up. I doubt it.”
“And how is Ilusha?”

“Ah, he’s bad, very bad! I think it’s consumption. He’s fully conscious, but his breathing! It’s gone all wrong. The other day he asked for his boots so someone could walk him around the room. He tried to walk and couldn’t even stand. ‘Ah, father,’ he said, ‘I told you before those boots were no good. I could never walk properly in them.’ He thought the boots were making him stagger, but it was only weakness, really. He won’t last another week. Herzenstube is treating him. And now they’re rich again—they’ve got heaps of money.”
“They’re rogues.”
“Who is?”

“Doctors. The whole gang of quacks, collectively and, of course, one by one. I don’t believe in medicine. It’s a useless institution. I intend to look into all of it. But what’s this sentimental business you’ve got going up there? The whole class seems to go every day.”
“Not the whole class. Only ten of us go and see him every day. That’s nothing special.”

“What I can’t make out in all this is the part Alexey Karamazov is playing. His brother is to be tried tomorrow or the day after for such a crime, and he still finds so much time for sentimentality with schoolboys.”
“It isn’t sentimentality. You’re on your way there yourself to make it up with Ilusha.”
“Make it up with him? What a ridiculous way to put it! And I don’t permit anyone to analyze my actions.”
“And Ilusha will be so happy to see you! He has no idea you’re coming. Why wouldn’t you come all this time, why?” Smurov cried with sudden warmth.

“My dear boy, that’s my business and not yours. I’m going of my own free will, because I choose to. The rest of you were all dragged there by Alexey Karamazov—there’s a difference, you know. And how do you know what I’m up to? Maybe I’m not going to make it up at all. It’s a stupid phrase.”

“It isn’t Karamazov at all. It’s not his doing. Our fellows started going there on their own. Of course, at first they went with Karamazov. But there was never any of that sort of thing—no silliness. One went, then another. His father was awfully glad to see us. You know, he’ll simply lose his mind if Ilusha dies. He can see Ilusha is dying. And he seems so glad we’ve made peace with Ilusha. Ilusha asked about you, that’s all. He only asks, and says nothing more. His father will go mad or hang himself. He acted like a madman before. You know, he’s a thoroughly decent man. We made a mistake back then. The whole fault lies with that murderer who beat him.”
“Karamazov is still a riddle to me. I could have got to know him long ago, but in some cases I like to keep a proper pride. Besides, I have a theory about him, and I have to work it out and test it.”

Kolya sank into a dignified silence. Smurov was silent too. Smurov, of course, worshiped Krassotkin and never dreamed of setting himself level with him. Now he was tremendously curious about Kolya’s saying he was “going of himself” to see Ilusha. He sensed there was some mystery behind Kolya’s suddenly deciding to visit him that day. They crossed the market square. At that hour it was full of loaded wagons from the country and a great number of live fowls. The market women sat in their booths selling rolls, cottons, threads and the like. These Sunday markets were naïvely called “fairs” in the town, and there were many such fairs in the year.

Perezvon ran about in the wildest spirits, sniffing first to one side, then to the other. Whenever he met other dogs, they went over each other eagerly with their noses, following the rules of canine etiquette.
“I like to watch such realistic scenes, Smurov,” Kolya said suddenly. “Have you noticed how dogs sniff each other when they meet? It seems to be a law of their nature.”
“Yes. It’s a funny habit.”

“No, it isn’t funny. You’re mistaken. There’s nothing funny in nature, however funny it may look to man with all his prejudices. If dogs could reason and criticize us, they’d certainly find just as much to laugh at in the social relations of men, their masters—more, in fact. Yes, I repeat it, because I’m convinced there’s far more foolishness among us than among them. That’s Rakitin’s idea, and a remarkable one. I’m a Socialist, Smurov.”
“And what’s a Socialist?” asked Smurov.

“It’s when everyone is equal and everyone owns everything together, there’s no marriage, and everyone has whatever religion and laws he likes best, and so on. You’re too young to understand that yet. It’s cold, though.”
“Yes, twelve degrees of frost. Father just looked at the thermometer.”

“Have you noticed, Smurov, that in the depth of winter, with fifteen or eighteen degrees of frost, we don’t feel as cold as we do now, at the start of winter, when a sudden frost of twelve degrees hits us, especially with so little snow? That’s because people aren’t used to it. With men, everything is habit—everything, even their social and political relations. Habit is the great driving force. What a funny-looking peasant!”

Kolya pointed to a tall, good-natured-looking peasant in a long sheepskin coat. He was standing by his wagon, clapping his hands together in their shapeless leather gloves to warm them. His long fair beard was white all over with frost.
“That peasant’s beard is frozen!” Kolya cried in a loud, provoking voice as he went by.
“Plenty of beards are frozen,” the peasant answered calmly and gravely.
“Don’t provoke him,” said Smurov.
“It’s all right. He won’t get angry. He’s a good fellow. Good-by, Matvey.”
“Good-by.”
“Is your name Matvey?”
“Yes. Didn’t you know?”
“No. It was a guess.”
“Well, I never! You’re a schoolboy, I take it?”
“Yes.”
“They whip you, I expect?”
“Nothing much—now and then.”
“Does it hurt?”
“Well, yes, it does.”
“Ech, what a life!” The peasant sighed from the bottom of his heart.
“Good-by, Matvey.”
“Good-by. You’re a fine lad, that you are.”
The boys walked on.
“Now there’s a good peasant,” Kolya said to Smurov. “I like talking to the peasants, and I’m always glad to do them justice.”
“Why did you lie and pretend we get thrashed?” asked Smurov.
“I had to, to please him.”
“How do you mean?”

“You know, Smurov, I don’t like being asked the same thing twice. I like people to catch on at the first word. Some things can’t be explained. In a peasant’s view, schoolboys get whipped, and have to be whipped. What kind of schoolboy wouldn’t be? And if I told him we aren’t, he’d be let down. But you don’t understand that. You have to know how to talk to the peasants.”
“Just don’t tease them, please, or you’ll land in trouble again, like with that goose.”
“So you’re scared?”
“Don’t laugh, Kolya. Of course I’m scared. My father would be furious. I’m strictly forbidden to go out with you.”
“Don’t worry, nothing will happen this time. Hello, Natasha!” he shouted to a woman in one of the market booths.
“Natasha, indeed! What next! My name is Marya,” the middle-aged woman shouted back at him.
“I’m so glad it’s Marya. Good-by!”
“Oh, you young rascal! A brat like you, carrying on like that!”
“I’m in a hurry, I can’t stay now. You can tell me next Sunday.” Kolya waved at her as if she had attacked him instead of the other way around.
“I’ve got nothing to tell you next Sunday. You started in on me, you cheeky young monkey. I never said a word,” bawled Marya. “What you want is a whipping, that’s what, you saucy jackanapes!”

The other market women around her roared with laughter. Suddenly a man darted out from the arcade of shops nearby, in a furious rage. He was young and not from the town, with dark curly hair and a long, pale, pockmarked face. He wore a long blue coat and a peaked cap and looked like a merchant’s clerk. He was stupidly worked up, and he shook his fist at Kolya.
“I know you!” he cried angrily. “I know you!”
Kolya stared at him. He couldn’t recall when he might have had a row with this man. But he’d been in so many street rows that he could hardly remember them all.
“Do you?” he asked sarcastically.
“I know you! I know you!” the man repeated idiotically.
“All the better for you. Well, I must be going. Good-by!”
“Up to your saucy tricks again?” cried the man. “Up to your saucy tricks again? I know it, you’re at it again!”
“It’s no business of yours, brother, whether I’m up to my tricks again,” said Kolya. He stopped and looked him up and down.
“No business of mine?”
“No. No business of yours.”
“Whose, then? Whose, then? Whose, then?”
“It’s Trifon Nikititch’s business, not yours.”
“What Trifon Nikititch?” asked the young man, gaping at Kolya with boorish amazement, but just as angry as before.
Kolya studied him gravely.
“Have you been to the Church of the Ascension?” he suddenly asked, with stern emphasis.
“What Church of the Ascension? What for? No, I haven’t,” said the young man, a little thrown.
“Do you know Sabaneyev?” Kolya went on, still more emphatically and still more sternly.
“What Sabaneyev? No, I don’t know him.”

“Then you can go to the devil,” said Kolya, ending the conversation. He turned sharply right and strode off, as if he would not lower himself to talk any longer with a dolt who didn’t even know Sabaneyev.
“Hold on, hey! What Sabaneyev?” The young man shook off his moment of stupefaction and was as worked up as before. “What did he say?” He turned to the market women with a foolish stare.
The women laughed.
“You never know what he’s getting at,” said one of them.
“What Sabaneyev is he talking about?” the young man repeated, still furious, swinging his right arm.
“Must be the Sabaneyev who worked for the Kuzmitchovs, that’s who it must be,” one of the women suggested.
The young man gave her a wild look.
“For the Kuzmitchovs?” another woman echoed. “But his name wasn’t Trifon. It’s Kuzma, not Trifon. And the boy said Trifon Nikititch, so it can’t be the same man.”

“It’s not Trifon and it’s not Sabaneyev, it’s Tchizhov,” a third woman put in suddenly. She had said nothing till then, and had been listening gravely. “Alexey Ivanitch is his name. Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch.”
“No doubt about it, it’s Tchizhov,” a fourth woman agreed firmly.
The bewildered young man looked from one to the other.
“But what was he asking, what was he asking, good people?” he cried, almost in despair. “‘Do you know Sabaneyev?’ he says. And who the devil would know who Sabaneyev is?”
“You’re a fool. I tell you it’s not Sabaneyev, it’s Tchizhov, Alexey Ivanitch Tchizhov, that’s who!” one of the women shouted at him, very earnestly.
“Which Tchizhov? Who is he? Tell me, if you know.”
“The tall one with the runny nose, who used to sit in the market in summer.”
“And what’s your Tchizhov to me, good people, eh?”

“How should I know what he is to you?” put in another. “You ought to know yourself what you want with him, if you’re making such a noise about him. He spoke to you, not to us, you fool. Don’t you really know him?”
“Know who?”
“Tchizhov.”
“The devil take Tchizhov, and you along with him. I’ll give him a hiding, that I will. He was laughing at me!”
“Give Tchizhov a hiding! More likely he’ll give you one. You’re a fool, that’s what you are!”
“Not Tchizhov, not Tchizhov, you spiteful, mischief-making woman. I’ll give that boy a hiding. Catch him, catch him, he was laughing at me!”

The woman guffawed. But Kolya was by now far away, marching on with a look of triumph. Smurov walked beside him, glancing back at the shouting group in the distance. He was in high spirits too, though he was still afraid of getting into some scrape in Kolya’s company.
“Which Sabaneyev did you mean?” he asked Kolya, already guessing the answer.

“How should I know? Now there’ll be an uproar among them all day. I like to stir up fools in every class of society. Look, there’s another blockhead, that peasant over there. You know the saying, ‘there’s no one stupider than a stupid Frenchman,’ but a stupid Russian shows it in his face just the same. Can’t you see it written all over his face that he’s a fool, that peasant, eh?”
“Leave him alone, Kolya. Let’s go.”
“Nothing could stop me now that I’ve started. Hey, good morning, peasant!”
A sturdy peasant with a round, simple face and a grizzled beard was walking past. He raised his head and looked at the boy. He seemed a bit drunk.
“Good morning, if you’re not making fun of me,” he answered slowly.
“And if I am?” laughed Kolya.
“Well, a joke’s a joke. Go on and laugh. I don’t mind. A joke does no harm.”
“Sorry, brother, it was a joke.”
“Well, God forgive you!”
“Do you forgive me, too?”
“I forgive you entirely. Go on your way.”
“I say, you seem like a clever peasant.”
“Cleverer than you,” the peasant answered unexpectedly, with the same gravity.
“I doubt it,” said Kolya, a little taken aback.
“It’s true, though.”
“Maybe it is.”
“It is, brother.”
“Good-by, peasant!”
“Good-by!”
“There are all kinds of peasants,” Kolya remarked to Smurov after a short silence. “How was I to know I’d picked a clever one? I’m always ready to acknowledge intelligence among the peasantry.”

In the distance the cathedral clock struck half-past eleven. The boys quickened their pace. They covered the long distance to Captain Snegiryov’s lodging fast and almost without a word. Twenty paces from the house Kolya stopped and told Smurov to go ahead and ask Karamazov to come out to him.
“First you have to sniff around a bit,” he told Smurov.
“Why ask him to come out?” Smurov objected. “Just go in. They’ll be awfully glad to see you. What’s the sense of making friends out here in the frost?”
“I know why I want to see him out here in the frost,” Kolya cut him short, in the despotic tone he liked to take with “small boys.” And Smurov ran off to do as he was told.
